lessons.title: Criteria for Selecting Steers for Fattening
lessons.body: When selecting steers for fattening, your goal is to buy animals that will gain weight quickly and efficiently. The best candidates are young, intact males (steers) that have been castrated early, typically before 6 months of age. Look for steers with a good appetite and a calm temperament. Age matters: steers between 12 and 24 months old are ideal because they are still growing and will put on muscle and fat rapidly. Avoid very old steers (over 3 years) as they convert feed less efficiently. Weight should be between 250 kg and 400 kg at purchase, depending on breed and target market. In Africa, common fattening breeds include Boran, Sahiwal, and crossbreeds with exotic breeds like Holstein or Angus. These breeds respond well to improved feeding. Health status is critical: only buy steers that are alert, have bright eyes, and no signs of diarrhea or coughing. Check for lameness and abscesses. Also consider the source: steers from known farms with vaccination records are safer than those from open markets where disease risk is higher. Finally, assess body condition: steers with a body condition score (BCS) of 2 to 3 on a 1-5 scale (where 1 is emaciated and 5 is obese) are ideal. They have some fat cover but are not overly fat, so they will gain efficiently. Avoid extremely thin steers (BCS 1) as they may have health issues and require costly recovery. Selecting the right steers at the start saves you money on feed and veterinary bills later.

lessons.title: Evaluating Body Condition and Frame Size
lessons.body: Body condition scoring (BCS) is a hands-on method to assess fat cover on a steer. Use a 1-5 scale: 1 = emaciated (bones prominent, no fat), 2 = thin (some fat over ribs, but ribs easily felt), 3 = moderate (ribs felt with slight pressure, fat cover over tailhead), 4 = fat (ribs hard to feel, fat deposits visible), 5 = obese (heavy fat cover, mobility issues). For fattening, aim for steers with BCS 2 to 3. They have enough energy reserves to start gaining but are not too fat, which would reduce feed efficiency. To check BCS, run your hands over the ribs, spine, and tailhead. Feel for the amount of fat. Also assess frame size: steers with a larger frame (taller, longer body) can grow to heavier weights before finishing. Frame score is often estimated by hip height at a given age. For example, a 12-month-old steer with a hip height of 120 cm is considered medium-frame; 130 cm is large-frame. In Africa, many local breeds are smaller-framed, but crossbreeds can be larger. Choose steers with a frame size that matches your market: if you sell to local butcheries, a 350-400 kg finished weight is fine; for premium markets, you may need 450-500 kg, requiring larger-framed steers. Also evaluate muscle thickness: look at the width of the stance, the roundness of the hindquarters, and the thickness of the forearm. A steer with good muscle and moderate fat will yield more meat. Remember, frame size and body condition together determine how long you need to feed and the final weight. Always handle the steers before purchase to evaluate both.

lessons.title: Assessing Health and Soundness
lessons.body: A healthy steer is a profitable steer. Before buying, inspect each animal carefully. Start with the eyes: they should be bright, clear, and free of discharge. Cloudy eyes or excessive tearing can indicate pinkeye or respiratory disease. Check the nose for discharge; a runny nose with coughing suggests pneumonia. Listen for breathing: normal breathing is quiet and regular. Rapid or labored breathing is a red flag. Examine the mouth for sores or excessive salivation, which could be foot-and-mouth disease. Look at the coat: it should be smooth and shiny. A dull, rough coat often means internal parasites or poor nutrition. Check the skin for lumps, wounds, or abscesses. Any open wound can become infected and reduce weight gain. Next, assess mobility: have the steer walk on a flat surface. It should move freely without limping. Lameness can be caused by foot rot, abscesses, or injuries, and will reduce feed intake. Inspect the hooves for cracks or swelling. Also check the anus for signs of diarrhea, which could be due to worms or bacterial infections. Finally, look at the overall posture: a healthy steer stands alert with head up. A depressed steer with droopy ears and head down is likely sick. In Africa, common diseases to watch for include East Coast fever (caused by ticks), trypanosomiasis (spread by tsetse flies), and foot-and-mouth disease. If possible, ask for vaccination records. If buying at a market, avoid animals that have been transported long distances and are stressed. Quarantine new steers for at least 14 days before mixing with your herd. During quarantine, observe them daily and treat any health issues immediately. A thorough health check saves you from buying a problem that will cost more than the steer itself.

lessons.title: Genetic Considerations and Expected Progeny Differences
lessons.body: Genetics determine how fast a steer grows, how efficiently it converts feed, and the quality of its meat. When selecting steers, you cannot change their genetics, but you can choose animals with superior genetic potential. In Africa, indigenous breeds like Boran, N'Dama, and Ankole have good heat tolerance and disease resistance but slower growth. Crossbreeds with exotic breeds like Angus, Hereford, or Simmental can grow faster and reach heavier weights. If you are buying steers for fattening, look for crossbreeds that combine local hardiness with exotic growth. Expected Progeny Differences (EPDs) are tools used by breeders to predict the genetic merit of an animal as a parent. For fattening steers, you are not breeding, but EPDs can still indicate the steer's own genetic potential for growth. Key EPDs include birth weight (lower is better for calving ease, but not relevant for steers), weaning weight (higher means faster early growth), yearling weight (higher means faster overall growth), and carcass weight (higher means more meat). If you buy from a registered breeder, ask for EPDs. For example, a steer with a yearling weight EPD of +30 kg is expected to be 30 kg heavier at one year than the breed average. However, EPDs are only useful if the breeder has accurate records. In many African markets, such data is scarce. Instead, you can assess genetics by looking at the steer's parents if available, or by choosing steers from herds known for good growth. Also consider hybrid vigor (heterosis): crossbred steers often outperform purebreds in growth and health. For small-scale fatteners, a simple strategy is to buy crossbred steers from reputable farms. Avoid mixing breeds with different mature sizes if you want uniform batches. Remember, genetics set the ceiling for performance; nutrition and management determine how close you get to that ceiling.

lessons.title: Purchasing Strategies: Auctions, Direct Sales, and Contracts
lessons.body: Where you buy your steers affects price, health, and convenience. Three common methods in Africa are auctions, direct sales, and contracts. Auctions: Livestock auctions are held in many towns. You can buy steers at competitive prices, but there are risks. Animals may be stressed from transport and mixing, increasing disease risk. You also have limited time to inspect. To succeed at auctions, arrive early, inspect animals before the sale, set a maximum price, and stick to it. Check for auctioneer fees (often 5-10% of the sale price). Direct sales: Buying directly from a farmer or feedlot allows you to inspect the animals in their home environment. You can negotiate price, ask about health and feeding history, and build a relationship. This is often the best option for beginners. Visit the farm, check records, and observe the steers. Agree on a price per kilogram live weight or per head. For example, in Kenya, a 300 kg steer might sell for KES 200-250 per kg live weight (about USD 1.50-2.00). Contracts: Some large feedlots or meat processors offer contract farming. You agree to raise steers to a certain weight and they buy at a predetermined price. This reduces market risk but may lock you into a low price. Contracts often require you to follow specific feeding and health protocols. Read the fine print. For all methods, ensure you get a receipt and health certificate if possible. Also consider transport costs: buying from a distant market may be cheaper but add transport and stress. Always quarantine new arrivals for 14 days. If buying in bulk, try to source from a single herd to reduce disease spread. Finally, timing matters: prices are often lower during dry seasons when farmers sell off animals. Buy then and fatten during the wet season when feed is cheaper.

lessons.title: Transport and Handling of Newly Purchased Steers
lessons.body: Transport is a critical period that can make or break your fattening operation. Stress during transport leads to weight loss, disease, and even death. Plan ahead to minimize stress. Before loading, ensure steers are healthy and have been off feed for 6-8 hours (but have access to water). This reduces defecation and urine in the truck. Use a well-ventilated truck with non-slip flooring. Cover the floor with sand or wood shavings for grip. Load steers calmly; shouting and hitting will stress them. Use flags or sticks to guide them. Do not overload: allow about 1.5 to 2 square meters per adult steer. For a 300 kg steer, that's roughly 1.5 mÂ². If traveling long distances (over 4 hours), stop every 4-6 hours to check animals and offer water. In hot African climates, transport during early morning or evening to avoid heat stress. Never transport in the heat of the day. If possible, use a truck with a roof for shade. During the journey, avoid sudden braking and sharp turns. Upon arrival, unload gently into a clean, dry quarantine pen. Provide fresh water and good quality hay. Do not feed concentrates immediately; wait 12-24 hours to avoid digestive upset. Observe for signs of stress: rapid breathing, drooling, or collapse. If any steer shows these, consult a vet. Keep new steers separate from your herd for at least 14 days. During quarantine, monitor temperature and appetite daily. Treat for internal and external parasites as advised by a vet. Vaccinate if not already done. Handle steers quietly and patiently; they learn routines. Use a race or crush for restraint when needed. Remember, good handling reduces bruises and injuries, which lowers meat quality. A calm steer gains weight faster. So invest time in proper transport and handling; it pays off in better health and performance.

quiz.q: What is the ideal age range for steers selected for fattening?
quiz.explanation: Steers between 12 and 24 months are still growing and convert feed efficiently.

quiz.q: Which body condition score (BCS) is ideal for purchasing steers for fattening?
quiz.explanation: BCS 2 to 3 indicates some fat cover but not excessive, allowing efficient weight gain.

quiz.q: What does a dull, rough coat on a steer often indicate?
options: B) Internal parasites or poor nutrition
quiz.explanation: A dull coat is a common sign of internal parasites or inadequate nutrition.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of respiratory disease in steers?
quiz.explanation: Coughing and nasal discharge are typical signs of pneumonia or other respiratory infections.

quiz.q: What is the recommended quarantine period for newly purchased steers?
quiz.explanation: A 14-day quarantine helps prevent the spread of diseases to your existing herd.

quiz.q: Which breed is known for heat tolerance and disease resistance in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Boran is an indigenous African breed adapted to local conditions.

quiz.q: What does a yearling weight EPD of +30 kg mean?
options: A) The steer weighs 30 kg at one year
B) The steer is expected to be 30 kg heavier than breed average at one year
C) The steer's mother weighed 30 kg more
D) The steer will gain 30 kg per day
quiz.explanation: EPDs predict genetic potential; a +30 kg yearling weight EPD means the steer is expected to be 30 kg heavier than average at one year.

quiz.q: What is hybrid vigor (heterosis)?
options: A) Crossbred offspring outperform purebreds in growth and health
D) A type of feed supplement
quiz.explanation: Hybrid vigor is the superior performance of crossbred animals compared to their purebred parents.

quiz.q: Which purchasing method allows you to inspect animals in their home environment?
quiz.explanation: Direct sales involve buying from a farm where you can see the animals and their conditions.

quiz.q: What is a common risk of buying steers at auctions?
quiz.explanation: Auctions often have time constraints, making it hard to thoroughly inspect animals.

quiz.q: How much space should be allowed per adult steer during transport?
quiz.explanation: 1.5 to 2 square meters per steer prevents overcrowding and stress.

quiz.q: What should you provide to steers immediately after transport?
quiz.explanation: Fresh water and hay help rehydrate and settle the rumen without causing digestive upset.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid transporting steers during the heat of the day?
options: C) Because trucks are not allowed
quiz.explanation: Heat stress can cause weight loss and even death; cooler times are safer.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of contract farming for steers?
quiz.explanation: Contracts set a predetermined price, reducing the risk of market fluctuations.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a healthy steer?
options: A) Droopy ears and head down
B) Bright eyes and alert posture
quiz.explanation: Bright eyes and alert posture indicate good health.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of body condition scoring (BCS)?
quiz.explanation: BCS is a hands-on method to evaluate the amount of fat on a steer.

quiz.q: What frame size is best for a market requiring 450-500 kg finished weight?
quiz.explanation: Large-framed steers can grow to heavier weights before finishing.

quiz.q: Which disease is spread by tsetse flies and affects steers in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness in animals) is transmitted by tsetse flies.

quiz.q: What should you do if a steer shows signs of stress after transport?
quiz.explanation: Stress can lead to disease; a vet can provide appropriate treatment.

quiz.q: Why is it important to handle steers calmly?
options: A) It reduces bruises and injuries
B) It makes them gain less weight
quiz.explanation: Calm handling reduces bruises and injuries, improving meat quality and weight gain.

quiz.q: What is the ideal weight range for purchasing steers for fattening?
quiz.explanation: 250-400 kg steers are still growing and respond well to fattening diets.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a criterion for selecting steers?
quiz.explanation: Coat color is not a primary criterion for fattening potential.

quiz.q: What does a BCS of 1 indicate?
quiz.explanation: BCS 1 means the steer is emaciated with no fat cover.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common internal parasite issue in steers?
quiz.explanation: Internal parasites like worms are common and cause poor growth.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of buying steers from a single herd?
quiz.explanation: Single-source herds reduce the risk of introducing multiple diseases.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy steers for fattening?
quiz.explanation: Prices are often lower during dry seasons when farmers sell off animals.

quiz.q: What should you check on a steer's feet during a health inspection?
quiz.explanation: Cracks or swelling can indicate foot rot or injury, leading to lameness.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an EPD?
quiz.explanation: EPDs estimate the genetic potential of an animal for traits like growth.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of foot-and-mouth disease?
options: B) Sores in mouth and salivation
quiz.explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease causes sores in the mouth and excessive salivation.

quiz.q: Why should you not feed concentrates immediately after transport?
options: C) Because they don't like it
quiz.explanation: Concentrates can cause acidosis if the rumen is not adapted; wait 12-24 hours.
